title: Design a Parking Lot: Vehicle types (car/bike/truck), ParkingSpot sizes, ParkingFloor, entry/exit gates, ticket system, payment, find nearest available spot.
topicTitle: LLD Problems: Parking Lot, Elevator, Chess, etc.
keyPoints: Vehicle types differ only in the spot size they need, modelled with an enum rather than deep inheritance.
A ParkingFloor holds spots and knows how to find the nearest free spot for a given vehicle size.
The ParkingLot orchestrator assigns a spot on entry, issues a ticket with entry time, and computes a fee on exit.
A FeeStrategy interface lets the lot support flat, hourly, or surge pricing without editing the lot code (Open/Closed Principle).
Thread safety is essential because two vehicles arriving simultaneously must never be assigned the same spot.
For scale, per-size priority queues keyed by distance replace linear scans for logarithmic lookup.
The design maps directly to assigning vault lockers at National Bank of India: size compatibility, concurrent allocation, and duration-based charging.

s1_definition.oneliner: A parking lot assigns the nearest compatible spot, issues a ticket, and charges by duration at exit.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Vehicle** – carries a `VehicleType` enum (BIKE, CAR, TRUCK) that determines the required spot size.
- **ParkingSpot** – has a size, a spot number, and an occupied flag; owns its own state transitions.
- **ParkingFloor** – holds a list of spots and provides `findNearestSpot(VehicleType)`.
- **ParkingLot** – the orchestrator that coordinates floors, issues tickets at entry, and computes fees at exit.
- **Ticket** – records entry time, assigned spot, and vehicle reference.
- **FeeStrategy** – a pluggable interface for flat, hourly, or surge pricing.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of the parking lot as the vault of National Bank of India where lockers come in three sizes. When Rajesh arrives with a small item he gets a small locker, Priya with a large item gets a large locker, the clerk writes a slip noting the entry time, and when they leave the cashier charges by the hours used. The parking lot assigns spots exactly like the bank assigns lockers.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Entry Flow:
  ───────────
  Vehicle arrives
       │
       ▼
  ParkingLot.entry(vehicle)
       │
       ▼
  ParkingFloor.findNearestSpot(type)
       │
       ▼
  ParkingSpot.occupy()   ← synchronized
       │
       ▼
  Issue Ticket(vehicle, spot, entryTime)
```

```text
  Exit Flow:
  ──────────
  Ticket presented
       │
       ▼
  ParkingSpot.free()
       │
       ▼
  FeeStrategy.computeFee(hours)
       │
       ▼
  Charge and release
```

```text
  ┌────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │            ParkingLot                   │
  │  entry(vehicle) → Ticket                │
  │  exit(ticket) → BigDecimal fee          │
  └──────┬──────────────────┬──────────────┘
         │                  │
         ▼                  ▼
  ┌──────────────┐   ┌──────────────┐
  │ ParkingFloor │   │ FeeStrategy  │
  │ findNearest()│   │ computeFee() │
  └──────┬───────┘   └──────────────┘
         │
         ▼
  ┌──────────────┐
  │ ParkingSpot  │
  │ occupy()     │
  │ free()       │
  └──────────────┘
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
When you design a parking lot, model it as a small set of cohesive classes rather than one giant manager. The core entities are Vehicle with a type that captures size, ParkingSpot that carries a size and an occupied flag, ParkingFloor that owns its spots and finds the nearest free compatible spot, Ticket that records the entry time, and ParkingLot that orchestrates entry and exit.

On entry, the lot walks its floors and asks each floor to find the nearest free spot of the right size. The allocation is thread-safe because two vehicles arriving at the same instant must never receive the same spot. Once a spot is reserved, a ticket is issued stamped with the entry time.

On exit, the lot computes the parked duration and applies a fee strategy. The fee strategy is deliberately pulled into an interface so the facility can switch from flat to hourly to surge pricing by adding a new class, never touching the orchestrator. That is the Open/Closed Principle paying off directly in a feature request.

For scale, replace the linear spot scan with per-size priority queues keyed by distance so lookups stay fast even with thousands of spots, and cache free-spot counts per floor for display boards. The design maps directly to assigning vault lockers at National Bank of India, where size compatibility, safe concurrent allocation, and duration-based charging are exactly the same concerns.

Remember one sentence: a parking lot assigns the nearest compatible spot atomically, issues a ticket with entry time, and charges by duration through a pluggable fee strategy.
